findings.source_passage: moody stricken Ahab stood before them with a crucifixion in his face; in all the nameless regal overbearing dignity of some mighty woe
findings.source_locator: paragraph describing Ahab's first appearance on deck, final sentence
findings.why_it_matters: The phrase 'nameless regal overbearing dignity of some mighty woe' is a critical-tradition keystone for Ahab's tragic grandeur; the draft preserves 'crucifixion in his face' but drops the crucial 'nameless regal overbearing dignity of some mighty woe,' cutting the interpretive weight of the passage in half.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'in all the nameless regal overbearing dignity of some mighty woe' immediately after 'a crucifixion in his face.'

findings.source_passage: as ever all clouds choose the loftiest peaks to pile themselves upon
findings.source_locator: penultimate paragraph, closing simile on Ahab's brooding during the passage
findings.why_it_matters: This is a textually distinctive, rhythmically memorable closing image that encodes Ahab's tragic elevation; its absence removes a voice-establishing metaphor that critics cite when discussing Melville's grandiloquent narrator.
findings.suggested_fix: Retain the cloud/peak simile when describing Ahab's brooding idleness: 'as ever all clouds choose the loftiest peaks to pile themselves upon.'

findings.source_passage: when with a fair wind the ship was rushing through the water with a vindictive sort of leaping and melancholy rapidity
findings.source_locator: second paragraph, describing the morning Ahab first appears
findings.why_it_matters: The phrase 'vindictive sort of leaping and melancholy rapidity' is prosodically and tonally distinctive Melville; it personifies the ship in a way that foreshadows the novel's themes and is irreducible to any paraphrase. The draft skips straight to 'foreboding shivers,' losing the atmospheric buildup.
findings.suggested_fix: Reinsert 'a vindictive sort of leaping and melancholy rapidity' when describing the ship's motion on that grey morning.

findings.source_passage: when the red-cheeked, dancing girls, April and May, trip home to the wintry, misanthropic woods; even the barest, ruggedest, most thunder-cloven old oak will at least send forth some few green sprouts
findings.source_locator: final paragraph, extended simile for Ahab's softening
findings.why_it_matters: The personification of April and May as 'red-cheeked, dancing girls' is voice-establishing in its whimsical extravagance; the draft jumps directly to the conclusion ('charmed him a little') without the elaborated oak simile, losing a characteristic register flourish.
findings.suggested_fix: Include at minimum the oak simile to preserve the tonal contrast between Melville's ornate imagery and Ahab's granite reserve.

summary: The draft preserves the skeleton of Chapter 28 but loses three medium-severity signature passages—'nameless regal overbearing dignity of some mighty woe,' 'all clouds choose the loftiest peaks,' and 'vindictive sort of leaping and melancholy rapidity'—which together constitute regenerable voice and interpretive-weight failures.
